title: When the Merge Coefficient Stops Mattering: Proximity Regularized Merging for Continual LoRA Adaptation
topic: General Machine Learning->Transfer, Multitask and Meta-learning
claim: A simple regularizing add-on consistently improves over the baseline across datasets and across alternative merge rules, without changing the rest of the pipeline.
layout: 2 radar panels side by side, shared legend style, red-vs-gray polygons on colored sectors
description: Two radar (spider) charts side by side. Panel (a), titled 'CLIP backbone: AAA across 7 settings', has seven axes labeled by dataset and task count (IN-R T=5/10/20, CIFAR T=10/20, DN T=5, CUB T=10). Panel (b), titled 'CLIP IN-R 10T: AAA across 7 merge rules', has seven axes for merge rules (P&M-Fisher, BECAME, P&M-fixed, Model-Avg, CoFiMA, CoMA, MagMax). Each chart has a gray polygon for the baseline (P&M Base / Base) and a red polygon for the proposed method (PRM / +Prox), with radial ticks from 60 to 90. The red polygon encloses the gray one on nearly every axis. Pastel colored wedges group the axes by dataset or rule family. The eye goes first to the red outlines bulging past the gray ones. Captions (a) and (b) sit beneath.
caption: Paired transfer checks for proximal task-vector shaping. (a) Dataset-level comparison on the CLIP backbone: PRM improves over the corresponding P&M Base across the plotted settings. (b) Merge-rule comparison on CLIP IN-R 10T: the same proximal task-vector-training term improves each reported Base→+Prox pair while leaving the write-in rule unchanged. Full values and setup checks are reported in Appendix D and Appendix C.
abstract: Rehearsal-free continual learning with parameter-efficient adapters can be cast as a sequence of task-vector write-in operations: for each new task, a low-rank adapter is learned and merged into a running model. We propose Proximity Regularized Merging (PRM), a minimal modification to sequential LoRA merging that adds a proximal penalty during task-vector training without changing the subsequent write-in rule. PRM acts as a robust task-vector regularizer: in the reported Base->+Prox diagnostics, it improves AAA across multiple write-in rules, backbones, and class-incremental settings, while its fixed-coefficient variant remains competitive with strong coefficient-based baselines. Mechanistically, matched-prefix norm controls and proximal-strength sweeps show that proximal training shrinks the task-vector radius, lowers Fisher-weighted interference, broadens the coefficient plateau, and exposes a stability-plasticity trade-off. Together, these results suggest that the effectiveness of sequential LoRA merging depends not only on how much of a task vector is written in, but also on whether the task vector itself has been trained to be mergeable.
